releases.title: Next Up 1.0: the guild’s game board, ready for the rotation

New: Next Up 1.0. Everything below already works and has been used by Post Nerf Clarity on a real board, on desktop and phone. This release adds no new features; it marks the board as ready.
Boards open by code: type one on the front page to open that board, or create it if it’s free. There are no accounts. Anyone with the code can use the board.

An optional password, chosen when the board is created. A password board shows nothing but a lock screen until it is unlocked, and this browser remembers the unlock until you press the lock on the code chip. The password can be changed later but never removed.
Three lanes, Up Next, Now Playing and Played. Drag cards between and within them with a mouse, by long-press on a phone, or with the keyboard.
Each card shows the game’s art and opens to its go-live date, server info (links work) and a sign-up list where anyone can add or remove players.
History logs every change with the name of whoever made it, and Restore undoes card edits, deletes, moves and removed sign-ups.
Live updates: changes show up for everyone viewing the board as they happen. If the connection drops, the board says so and pauses editing until it’s back.

Settings: pick one of five themes (Light, Dark, Legacy, Pastel, Cyberpunk, or Match device), set your display name, and for the board you came from, change its password or delete it. A deleted board can be restored for 24 hours, then it and its code are gone.

Card art for 31 games: 7 Days to Die, Abiotic Factor, ARK: Survival Ascended, Conan Exiles, Core Keeper, DayZ, Don’t Starve Together, Dune: Awakening, Enshrouded, Everwind, Factorio, Hytale, ICARUS, Minecraft, Night of the Dead, Once Human, Palworld, Pax Dei, Project Zomboid, Rust, Satisfactory, Sons of the Forest, Soulmask, Space Engineers, Stardew Valley, Stormforge, Subnautica 2, Terraria, Unturned, V Rising and Valheim. Pick one from a card’s logo list.

releases.title: Hardening before the guild test: nightly backups, safer headers, clearer states, better keyboard use

New: Nightly backups. Every night at 04:00 UTC the database is copied to the backups share on <HOST>, checked for corruption before it is kept, and named by date. The last 30 days are kept. A backup that fails says so loudly in the web container’s log, and the earlier ones stay. RESTORE.md walks through putting one back.

The web app now says in its log which connection address the visitor-address header arrives from, so the rate limits can be told to trust only the tunnel (TRUSTED_PROXIES). README “Rate limits behind the tunnel” has the steps.
Improved: Security headers on every page and answer: a Content-Security-Policy that allows only Next Up’s own scripts, styles, fonts and images, no framing by other sites, no sniffing, no referrer (a board’s address holds its code), and every device permission (camera, microphone, location and the rest) switched off.
Repeat visits load faster: the app’s files are cached by the browser until they change, instead of being checked again on every visit.

Keyboard use: focus now lands somewhere sensible everywhere. A board opened from the landing page or a lock screen focuses the board; closing a dialog goes back to what opened it (or to History, after a restore); removing a player moves to the next one; a wrong password selects it to retype; “too many tries” moves to the message.
Screen readers hear the value on the Lane, Logo and Go-live buttons (“Lane, Up Next”), not just their label.
Reduce motion is fully respected: with it on, sheets and pages fade in instead of sliding or rising, and the live dot and loading shimmer hold still.
A board that couldn’t load now says “Timed out after 10 s” when that’s what happened, and offers Back to Home.
Text that was too faint is now readable (4.5:1 or better): the deleting countdown banner’s text in Light and Pastel, and the next and previous month’s days in the date picker in every theme.
Drag auto-scroll near the top of the window now starts below the top bar, not underneath it.
Fixed: If reloading a board failed after it fell behind (many changes while disconnected), the top bar still said Live and editing stayed on. It now says “Out of date”, pauses editing, and Retry reloads it.
A board’s whole History could show its loading shimmer for ever if the board had been erased meanwhile. It now says it couldn’t load.

Failures that were silent now say what happened: removing a player, deleting a card while the board is being deleted, and deleting, restoring or changing the password of a board when the server answers unexpectedly.
The lock screen now says “You’re offline” when you are, instead of “Couldn’t check it”.
Inside a card or a confirmation, “You’re offline” no longer showed as “Reconnecting…” while still connected.
A board that couldn’t load no longer shows “Connecting…” in the top bar.
A server error’s log line no longer includes the board’s code.
Removed: The leftover “coming soon” page and its “isn’t built yet” wording. Unknown addresses still get “Page not found”.

releases.title: Claude can read open boards through the MCP server

New: The MCP server (on the home network only, port 3231, with its bearer token) has three new read-only tools, so Claude can answer questions like “what's up next on pnc-raids, and who's signed up for Dune?” mid-conversation.

get_board reads a board by its code: the three lanes in order, and in each its cards top to bottom with title, logo, go-live date and how many players have signed up. An empty lane says it's empty. A board being deleted says when it will be erased.

get_card reads one card in full: lane and position, go-live date, server info exactly as typed, the players in sign-up order, and when it was made and last edited. Name the card by its id or its exact title (case doesn't matter). If two cards share that title, it lists both instead of guessing.
get_history reads a board's change log, newest first, worded exactly as the History panel words it, with who and when. 20 changes at a time by default, up to 100, with a cursor to read further back.
Boards with a password stay closed to the MCP. Every tool answers only “locked” for them: no name, cards, counts, logos, players, dates or history. There's no way to give the MCP a password.

You have to give the MCP a board's code. It can't list, search or guess codes, and nothing it says ever mentions a code you didn't give it. It still can't change anything: its connection to the database refuses every write.

releases.title: This board: change a board's password, or delete a board with 24 hours to undo it

New: Settings has a “This board” section when you open Settings from a board you're in. It isn't there when you open Settings from the front page or from a lock screen.

Change a board's password: type the current one, then the new one twice (8 to 128 characters, as when a board is made). Next Up asks you to confirm first. This browser stays in. Everyone else, including anyone with the board open at that moment, goes straight to “The board’s password changed” and needs the new one. History records who changed it and when, never the password, and it can't be undone from History. An open board still can't get a password, and a password still can't be removed.

Wrong current passwords in Settings count against the same limit as the lock screen: 10 wrong tries from your network in 15 minutes, wherever they happen, then a “Too many tries for now” countdown in both places.

Delete a board from Settings by typing its code. Nothing is erased straight away. For 24 hours the board shows “This board will be deleted in 23h 12m.” with a live countdown and a Restore button, for everyone who opens it and for anyone already looking at it. Cards, players, details, dragging and History's Restore are paused, but the board, its cards and History can still be read. A board with a password still needs it.
Restore puts the board back to normal with one click and a confirmation, and anyone who can open the board can do it during those 24 hours. History shows who deleted the board and who restored it.

After 24 hours the board is erased for good: every card, player and line of its history. Its code is free again, and the old link shows the normal “create it?” page. Until then the code stays taken, and the board still counts towards Next Up's 500-board limit.
Improved: The create-a-board screen no longer says changing the password is “coming soon”.

releases.title: Live sync: everyone sees changes as they happen

New: Boards update live. When anyone adds, edits, moves or deletes a card, changes a go-live date or server info, signs up or removes a player, or restores something from History, everyone else with the board open sees it within a moment, without reloading. An open card panel and an open History panel update in place too.

A card someone else just changed lights up for a couple of seconds with a name tag saying who and what, such as “Bunzato moved this” or “Kaelis added player Mo”. Screen readers hear the change read out. With reduced motion on, the highlight shows and goes without animating.

A sync pill next to the board code says whether the board is live: “Live”, “Connecting…”, “Reconnecting…”, “Offline · as of 14:32” or “Not connected · as of 14:32”. It only says Live while Next Up is actually getting through. On a phone it shrinks to a dot or an icon.

When the connection drops (a network change, a laptop waking from sleep, Next Up restarting for an update), the board says so, shows how old it is, and pauses editing with “Editing paused until we reconnect.” and a Retry button. It reconnects by itself, and when it's back it catches up on exactly the changes it missed, once each. If it has missed a great many, it reloads the board instead.
Improved: If someone else changes a card while you're dragging, nothing moves under you: their changes wait until you let go. If they delete the card you're holding, the drag is cancelled and a message says who deleted it.

If someone else changes a card while you're editing it, what you've typed stays put. The edit sheet says “Changed by Bunzato” with a “Load their changes” button, and saving still checks for their change first, so nothing is overwritten without you seeing it.
If someone else deletes a card whose panel or edit sheet you have open, it says who deleted it, rather than showing details that are no longer there, and points to History to bring it back.
Fixed: The edit sheet and the delete confirmation no longer say deleted cards can be restored “once History is built”. History has been here since 0.7.0.

releases.title: History and Restore, and glass that looks like glass

New: History: the clock button in the top bar opens the board's history, newest first, 50 changes at a time with “Load more” for older ones. Each line says who did what, for example “Bunzato moved Valheim · Now Playing → Played” or “Path removed player Larias from V Rising”, grouped under Today, Yesterday and earlier dates. Today's changes say how long ago they happened (“12 min ago”); hover over a time, or tap or long-press it on a phone, to see the exact date and time. Changes made without a display name show as “Someone”. Names are whatever each browser typed, and History says so.
“This card's history” in a card's panel opens History showing only that card's changes, with a button to widen it to the whole board. Closing it takes you back to the card.

Restore: card edits (name and logo), go-live date and server info changes, moves, deleted cards and removed players each have a Restore button. Restoring first shows what will change, with what the card has now beside what it will have afterwards, and only then does it. Like any change, it asks a browser that has never given a display name for one first.

A restore never deletes or rewrites anything in History. It makes the change and adds a new line, such as “Path moved Valheim back to Now Playing, 1st”, which says whose change it undid. That line has its own Restore, so a restore can be undone too. The change that was restored is marked “Restored” with who did it and when, and can't be restored a second time.

Restoring is careful when the board has moved on. If a card has been edited again since, only the fields that change touched go back and the rest stay as they are now. If its old lane has changed, it goes as close to its old place as the lane allows, and the confirmation says so. If the card has been deleted since, Restore offers to bring the card back too. It refuses, and says why, when a player of that name has signed up again, when the board already has 200 games, when the card already has 100 players, or when there is nothing left to undo. If someone else changes the card while the confirmation is open, it shows the new confirmation instead of restoring something you didn't agree to.
Improved: The glass looks like glass. Dark and Light now have soft colour behind them (blue, rose, teal and a warm glow) for the lanes and bars to blur, every glass panel has a fine edge and a bright line along its top, and Light's panels are clearer instead of nearly solid white. The top bar now stays at the top of the screen as frosted glass, and the board scrolls underneath it and under the bottom bar. Text on the glass was measured at 4.5:1 contrast or better in every theme. Legacy stays flat and solid by design, cards with no logo keep their solid colour, and Pastel and Cyberpunk keep their look.
The version number and “What's new” moved onto the bottom bar, on the left, with “Buy me a coffee” on the right. On a phone both fit on one line.
Removed: The separate version line under the board, now that the version is on the bottom bar.

releases.title: Card details: go-live date, server info and sign-ups

New: A card can have a go-live date. Set it in the card's edit sheet with a calendar that matches your theme, with “Today” and “Clear date” buttons. It's a date only, with no time: “Sat 24 Oct” is the same day for everyone, wherever they live. The card's panel shows the date and how far away it is (“In 9 days”, “Goes live today”, “Live 12 days”), and the card on the board shows it as a small badge. A card without a date says “Not set” in its panel and shows no badge.

A card can hold server info: one free-text box, up to 2,000 characters, for addresses, ports, passwords, mod lists and links. Web addresses starting with http:// or https:// become links that open in a new tab; everything else, including anything that looks like HTML or markdown, is shown exactly as typed. “Copy all” copies the whole text. Anyone who can open the board can read it, so a password board's server info is only as private as its password.

Sign up for a game: “Add Player” in a card's panel opens a box filled in with your display name (change it to add someone else) and Add puts the name on the card, in the order people signed up. Enter adds and keeps the box open for the next name. A name already on the card is turned away, whatever its capitals; a card holds up to 100 players. Anyone with the board can remove any name with the × on it, straight away and without a confirmation. The card on the board shows how many people are signed up.
Adding a player counts as a change, so a browser that has never given a display name is asked for one first, like any other change.

Every change to a card's date and server info, every sign-up and every removal is recorded in the board's history with what it was before, so the coming History page can undo edits and put removed players back where they were. History itself isn't built yet.
Improved: A card's panel now shows its date, server info and players instead of the list of its lane, logo and dates. Its lane is still on the card at the top, and when it was added is at the bottom.

New: Drag a card to move it: up or down within its lane, or into another lane at any position. The card lifts and tilts as you pick it up, a slot opens where it will land, and the cards around it slide apart to make room. Let go to drop it; press Escape to put it back. Dropping it where it started changes nothing.

On a phone, press and hold a card for a moment to pick it up, then drag it. Hold it near the top or bottom of the screen and the page scrolls toward the lane you want; that lane's heading lights up, says “Drop here” and shows its new count, and a note at the bottom says where the game will land. A quick tap still opens the card, and swiping still scrolls the board. The Lane option in a card's edit sheet is still there if you'd rather not drag.

Move cards from the keyboard: Tab to a card, press Space to pick it up, use the up and down arrows to move it within its lane and left and right to move it between lanes, then Space or Enter to drop it, or Escape to cancel. Screen readers hear each step, for example “Lifted Valheim. Up Next, position 2 of 5.”

Every move is recorded in the board's history with where the card was and where it went, so a later History page can put it back. Moving a card with the edit sheet's Lane option is recorded as a move too. If two people move the same card at the same moment, the later move wins and both are recorded; the other person sees the result when they next load the board.
A “Buy me a coffee” link to support Next Up now sits in a thin bar along the bottom of every page. It's a plain link that opens Buy Me a Coffee in a new tab; nothing from that site loads in Next Up.

A board is now a real board: three lanes, Up Next, Now Playing and Played, side by side on a computer and stacked top to bottom on a phone, each with its number of games. A brand-new board says so and offers “Add a game”; an empty lane says it has nothing in it yet.

Add a game with the + on any lane: type its name (up to 60 characters), optionally pick a logo, and choose the lane. New games go to the bottom of their lane. A board holds up to 200 games; when it's full it says so and asks you to delete one first.

Each game is a wide pill card. With a logo, the logo fills the card behind the name. Without one, the card is a solid colour from your theme with the game's name and its initials in a small disc. If a card's logo is ever removed from Next Up, the card quietly shows the plain colour instead of a broken image.

Click a card (or reach it with Tab and press Enter) to open it: its name, logo, lane and when it was added, with Edit and Delete. Editing lets you rename it, change its logo, or move it to another lane, where it goes to the bottom. Delete asks first.

The logo dropdown searches Next Up's logo library and shows each game with a small preview, with “No logo” always first. The library is empty for now, and the dropdown says so. Picking a logo for an untitled card fills in the game's name, which you can still change. Logos are added to the library by Path; nobody can upload images.

The first time this browser changes anything (creating a board counts), Next Up asks who you are, so the board's history can say who changed what. It's a label, not an account. “Not now” is remembered: your changes show as “Someone” and it won't ask again here. You can set or change the name any time in Settings.

Every add, edit and delete is recorded in the board's history with what the card was before and after, so a later History page can undo them. Deleted cards are kept, not erased. History itself isn't built yet, so there is no way to restore one from the app today.
If someone else changes a card while you're editing it, saving doesn't overwrite their change: Next Up shows their version and asks you to make yours again.
Improved: If your connection drops, the board says you're offline, shows the board as it was and when it was loaded, and pauses adding and editing until you reconnect, with a Retry button. If a save can't reach Next Up, the sheet says nothing was saved and keeps what you typed.
If a password board is locked from another tab, or its password changes, while you have it open, your next change takes you back to its lock screen instead of failing.
Fixed: Glass panels, sheets and the blurred backdrop behind dialogs had no blur in Chrome and Edge on the live site (the published build dropped the setting those browsers read). They now blur as designed.

New: Boards exist. Type a code on the front page: if the board exists it opens (or shows its lock screen); if nobody has used the code yet, Next Up offers to create it. Codes are 3 to 32 letters, numbers and hyphens, and capital letters don't matter: PNC-Raids and pnc-raids are the same board. Each board has its own address, /b/<code>.

When you create a board you choose, once, whether it has a password. Without one, anyone with the code can open and edit it, for good: a password can't be added later. With one, the code alone shows only a lock screen; the password will be changeable later but can never be removed, and it can't be recovered. You type it twice when creating the board.

The lock screen asks for the password and says plainly when it's wrong. Once it's right, this browser remembers the board until you press the lock on the code chip in the top bar, which forgets it here (no one else is affected). If the board's password has changed since this browser last opened it, the lock screen says so and asks for the new one.
The top bar shows the board's code with a copy button that copies the board's link (never the password). On a lock screen it shows only the code you typed.
Opening a board shows what is real so far: that it's open, whether it has a password and when it was made. Lanes and cards are not built yet, and the page says so instead of showing anything made up.

Abuse limits, per network: 10 wrong passwords per 15 minutes across all boards, and 30 codes that don't exist (or board creations) per 15 minutes. Past either, Next Up shows a countdown until you can try again. Boards this browser has opened before still open by their link while the code limit is in force.
Next Up holds at most 500 boards. When it is full, a free code says so straight away instead of letting you fill in the form first. Opening existing boards still works.

Every board keeps a change history from the moment it is created, recording who made each change by their display name (or "Someone" if they haven't set one). It isn't shown anywhere yet; it is what History and Restore will read. Password changes will be recorded without the password itself.
Improved: If Next Up can't be reached while opening, creating or unlocking, it says so and keeps what you typed, separately from "wrong password" or "nothing here".

New: Settings now has a theme picker: Light, Dark, Legacy, Pastel and Cyberpunk, each shown as a small preview, plus Match device, which uses Light or Dark and follows your device when it switches. The change applies at once with a short cross-fade and is remembered in this browser only.

Settings has a display name field. It is kept in this browser only and is a label, not an account: anyone can type any name. Nothing uses it yet; it is for the change history that comes with boards. Until you set one it says Not set.
If your browser blocks Next Up from saving anything, Settings says so, and your theme and name still work until you close or reload the page.
Improved: Every page now uses the Next Up design: its colours, buttons, fields and badges, in all five themes.
Legacy is now the flat theme: solid surfaces with no blur or see-through glass, crisp 1 px edges, small corners and squared-off buttons, so it no longer looks like a darker copy of Dark.
Buttons and the settings, back and What's new links have touch targets at least 44 px tall, so they are easier to hit on a phone.
The top bar shows the Next Up mark next to the name, and the board code box uses a code-style font.

New: Next Up exists, but boards don't yet. The front page has the box where you'll type a board's code; pressing Enter goes to that board's address, which says plainly that boards are coming soon. Nothing is created or saved when you do this.
Every page has a bottom bar with the version number. Clicking it opens What's new: this list.

A settings button in the top right opens a Settings page that says what will live there: your theme and your display name, both kept in this browser only. Neither can be changed yet. The page follows your device's light or dark mode until the theme picker exists.
An AI access point (MCP) that reads and never changes anything. It needs a bearer token and has one tool so far, get_version, which reports the running version.

Behind the scenes: pushing to main rebuilds and restarts Next Up on <HOST>, and the deploy fails if either container doesn't answer its health check, keeps restarting, or reports a different version than this list. The deploy never touches the server's .env file, and checks that it didn't.
